title: A Whole new world
paragraphs: "A vague longing for foreign countries and for studying abroad. I want to experience an unknown world." I first began to feel this way in my first year, when I learned that Nagoya University had an exchange program. Five years passed in a flash, and now that I am back in Japan, I feel that my three months in the United States gave me more than I had expected. I did my clinical clerkships at Johns Hopkins University, its main hospital Johns Hopkins Hospital, and the affiliated Bayview Medical Center. It is one of the leading medical schools in the United States, a university of a high standard in both clinical work and research, and also a hospital that deals every day with gunshot wounds and AIDS. I think I was able to make good use of this environment in my own way during the three months of clerkship. What I learned here was both about the system and about the diversity of diseases. First, the difference in the system. In three months I rotated through three departments: nephrology, endocrinology and infectious diseases. In general hospitals in the United States, unlike in Japan, each department does not have its own ward. Instead, residents belong to the general medicine ward and manage patients comprehensively, and when a problem arises that they cannot handle, they ask each department for a consult. I also belonged to a consult team. Every day I examined patients on the wards, presented to the fellows (specialty trainees) and attendings (supervising physicians), and thought through the plan and assessment together with them. Comparing this with Japan, I made various discoveries. First, as a resident or student, many healthcare professionals are involved with a single patient, so presentation skills are necessary, and in addition you can receive teaching from people in each field and from various angles. There are not only doctors but also many kinds of other healthcare professionals, and in endocrinology I even had the opportunity to attend a lecture by a diabetes nurse specialist. Also, specialist physicians who do not need to manage a ward can devote time to research and teaching. Students also have responsibilities and a lot is asked of them. Going to the ward alone, introducing myself to the patient, examining them and asking the ward staff about the patient's condition was unthinkable in my clerkships in Japan, so at first I even hesitated to enter a patient's room. Patients, doctors and other healthcare professionals also speak to me without hesitating (or perhaps without noticing?) that I am a student or a foreigner. Compared with Japan, there was more responsibility and more was asked of me. However, after about a month, I noticed that I was entering patients' rooms without resistance and phoning the ward, and I realized that I was growing little by little. On the other hand, I also felt that being allowed to do so many things as a student is linked to the evaluation of one's future. The strictness of being checked in detail with evaluation forms was also something that does not exist in Japan. Faced with that strictness, I cannot count how many times I felt frustrated by my own lack of ability. And the diversity of the diseases I saw was striking. In the consult service I saw different patients every day, so the number of cases I experienced was itself large, and I saw many diseases that one does not see in Japan: diseases related to race, such as sickle cell disease and cystic fibrosis, diseases related to social background, such as drug addiction and HIV/AIDS, and the many diseases caused by obesity. Infectious diseases in particular is a department that does not exist in Japan, so the diseases I saw there and the way of thinking were all new and interesting. On the other hand, every time I saw diseases based on social background and obesity, and the problems of health insurance, I often realized the strengths of Japanese medicine.

And the greatest asset of this study abroad was the people I met. The many patients who kindly let me examine them in my daily clerkship, the fellow with whom I got through the especially demanding nephrology rotation, and the many people I met outside the clerkship. As is probably true of the United States in general, Johns Hopkins was a mix of many nationalities and ethnicities. Each person was doing interesting work, some in basic research and some in clinical practice, and talking with them was the most stimulating thing. There is also a School of Public Health next to the hospital, and seeing people who had come from many countries to study public health trying to use what they researched there for the health of the world felt to me as if the whole world were spread out right there. I sincerely thank them for these encounters. And whatever the field, I strongly wish to study again in such an environment. This study abroad was truly a whole new world for me, and I was able to have a fulfilling experience thanks to the support of many people. I thank the staff of the International Exchange Office who gave me this opportunity for study abroad, Dr. 小林孝彰, Dr. 伊藤勝基, Ms. 鈴木, Ms. 西尾, Dean Dr. 濵口, my family, and my classmates.
